decisions.quote: The results of the study preliminarily suggest that, unlike the reference study, L2 proficiency level does not have a considerable effect on the acquisition order of morphemes.
decisions.reason: The thesis title and main research question focus on the effect of L2 proficiency level on morpheme acquisition order, which failed to replicate the reference study's finding of significant differences between beginner and intermediate learners. For the secondary research question on developmental error patterns across proficiency levels, the author likewise did not recover the reference study's U-shaped regular past pattern or article error distribution and concluded that low frequencies prevented answering that question completely, so a minor descriptive similarity in irregular-past misuse types does not make the replication outcome mixed.

parent_objection: First reply treats paper main RQ1 failure as overall failed, but source Conclusions Table5 and text identify multiple agreements and contrasts with the exact reference study. It says irregular past misuse errors were reported to be similar to current study (Lozano and Diaz-Negrillo2019,p110), while other original patterns differ. Codebook Rule1 genuine overall replication verdict versus single finding; otherwise Rule2 all original-specific comparisons count. Does the abstract claim about proficiency affect only focal RQ1 rather than overall outcome? Inspect Conclusion Table5, RQ2 shared irregular-past result, and distinguish agreements with generic previous MOS from agreement with actual replicated original. Do not dismiss a tested original finding as minor without codebook support. Resolve successful/mixed/failed using author comparisons, not our own tally of significance.

blind_target.title: Using learner corpus methods in L2 acquisition research.
blind_target.evidence_quote: The aim of the current study is to replicate Lozano and Díaz-Negrillo’s reference study using a different dataset.
blind_target.outcome_quote: The reference study did not look into NTLU of 3rd person singular -s because of its low frequency, but the misuse errors for irregular past were reported to be similar to the current study (Lozano and Díaz-Negrillo 2019, 110). While the reference study discovered a partial U-shaped developmental pattern in the oversuppliance of regular past -ed (Lozano and Díaz-Negrillo 2019, 111), the current study 44 did not show such a pattern for this or any other morpheme.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: No single overall replication verdict. The author explicitly reports both matching irregular-past error patterns and failure to recover the original U-shaped regular-past pattern. The central proficiency-order effect and article-error distribution also differ from the reference study. These are the two stated replication research questions, not incidental robustness analyses. Low frequencies limit some patterns but the author does not declare the entire attempt incapable of adjudication.
